scenes.headline: Virtual Environments & pip
scenes.subtitle: Isolated, reproducible dependencies
scenes.narration: Virtual environments keep each project's packages separate, while pip installs those packages from the Python Package Index.

scenes.headline: Why isolate dependencies
scenes.narration: Different projects often need different, sometimes conflicting versions of the same library, and a virtual environment gives each one its own private set. Recording those exact versions makes the install reproducible, so a teammate or a server ends up with the same setup you have. Isolation also keeps the system Python untouched, avoiding the mess that comes from installing everything globally. Pinning the versions in a requirements file turns your dependencies into something you can commit and repeat.

scenes.headline: Create, activate, install
scenes.code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install pandas
pip freeze > requirements.txt
scenes.narration: The first command creates a fresh virtual environment in a folder named dot venv. Activating it points your shell at that environment's own Python and pip. We then install pandas, which lands inside the environment rather than system-wide. Finally, pip freeze writes the exact installed versions into requirements dot txt so the setup can be recreated anywhere.

scenes.headline: The typical setup workflow
scenes.narration: The standard workflow starts by creating a virtual environment for the project and then activating it. With the environment active you install the packages you need, all captured in that isolated space. As a final step you freeze the installed versions to a requirements file, locking in reproducibility.

scenes.headline: Global versus virtual environment
scenes.narration: Installing packages globally means every project shares one pile of dependencies, so upgrading a library for one project can quietly break another. It also makes the setup hard to reproduce on a fresh machine. A per-project virtual environment isolates each set of dependencies, eliminating those clashes and making the whole thing reproducible from the requirements file.

scenes.text: Always work inside a virtual environment and pin dependencies with requirements.txt for reproducible builds.
scenes.narration: The takeaway is to always work inside a virtual environment and to pin your dependencies in a requirements file, which makes your projects reproducible on any machine.
